questions.answer: It uses the sound and shape of its lines to make the feeling of fear and courage come alive.

questions.skill: Reading fantasy and science fiction settings

questions.skill: How world rules make fantasy/science fiction settings believable

questions.skill: Recognizing text structures
questions.prompt: Read the sentences: "The town built a new dam to hold back floodwater. As a result, farms downstream stayed dry during the spring storms. However, the river below the dam later ran too low for fish to spawn." Which text structure does this passage mainly use?

Chronological order
Compare and contrast
Problem and solution

questions.answer: Bicycles changed over time, from simple machines pushed by foot to the familiar design used today.
choices: Bicycles changed over time, from simple machines pushed by foot to the familiar design used today.

Bicycles were invented in the 1890s and quickly became popular around the world.

questions.skill: Author's purpose and perspective

choices: To argue against the bike path, using the viewpoint of a lifelong resident who loves the dunes.
To inform readers how bike paths are built, using the viewpoint of a city engineer.
To tell the history of the town, using the viewpoint of a visiting tourist.
To entertain readers with a story, using the viewpoint of a young child.

questions.skill: Comparing multiple accounts

One of the authors must have written about a completely different town.

questions.skill: Combining information from several sources
questions.prompt: A student is researching how volcanoes form. She reads a science textbook chapter, watches a short video of a volcano erupting, and reads a website article from a university. What should she do to build knowledge on the topic?

choices: Pull the key facts from each source and combine them into one clear explanation of how volcanoes form.

questions.answer: To persuade readers that class sizes should be smaller, drawing on the author's experience as a teacher.
choices: To persuade readers that class sizes should be smaller, drawing on the author's experience as a teacher.
To describe in a neutral way what a typical school day looks like for a teacher.

To report the exact number of students in classrooms across the state this year.

questions.skill: Combining information across sources
questions.prompt: A student is writing a report about the history of hot-air balloons and finds: (1) a museum website article about the first balloon flight in France in 1783, and (2) a book about early air travel that describes the same flight but focuses on how crowds reacted. questions.answer: Combine the facts from both sources, noting where they agree and where one gives extra details the other leaves out.
choices: Combine the facts from both sources, noting where they agree and where one gives extra details the other leaves out.
Use only the museum website, because websites are always more accurate than books.

questions.skill: Identifying claims, reasons, and evidence
questions.prompt: Read the text: "Our school should add a second lunch period. Right now, students have only fifteen minutes to eat, which is not enough time for a full meal. questions.answer: The claim is that the school should add a second lunch period, supported by the reason that fifteen minutes is not enough time to eat.
choices: The claim is that the school should add a second lunch period, supported by the reason that fifteen minutes is not enough time to eat.
The claim is that students should eat faster, supported by the reason that lunch periods are too long.

questions.skill: Supported vs. unsupported claims
questions.prompt: Read the two sentences: "Our city should build more bike lanes. Building them is a good idea because everyone agrees it will make the city better." Which statement best describes the second sentence?

choices: It gives a reason that is not supported, because it offers no facts or examples to back it up.

questions.skill: Memoir vs. biography

The memoir focuses only on the woman's adult life, while the biography covers only her childhood.
The memoir uses dialogue and description, while the biography is written as a list of dates.
The memoir is written for children, while the biography is written for scholars only.

questions.skill: Telling evidence from claim and reasoning in an argument
questions.prompt: Read the text: "Our town library should stay open later on weeknights. choices: The detail that students finish sports practice after 5 p.m. and the library closes at 6 p.m.
The statement that the library should stay open later on weeknights.

questions.skill: Memoir vs. biography: how presentation differs
questions.prompt: One book is a memoir in which a man describes his own years as a sailor, using his memories and feelings. choices: The memoir describes his fear and what the storm felt like from the inside, while the biography explains what happened based on records and other people's accounts.
The memoir avoids any mention of feelings and lists only the dates and facts of the voyage.

questions.skill: Postcolonial subtext and voice
questions.prompt: Read this sentence: "When the district officer explained the new tax, we smiled and agreed, because our fathers had learned what happens to those who say no." In context, the people's agreement is best described as which of the following?

questions.skill: Translation choices and trade-offs
questions.prompt: A poem written in French in 1920 is reprinted in an English textbook. questions.skill: Feminist reading of whose voice dominates

questions.skill: Multiple Interpretations of One Work
questions.prompt:
At the end of a play, Elias hands Marta a letter. She reads it, says "Then it is decided," and walks to the door as the lights fade. Two stagings of this scene were filmed:

questions.prompt:

"The tide, that flat brass light, went out and out;

titles: How Authors Define and Refine Key Terms
Tracing Complex Ideas and Events Through a Long Text

questions.skill: Rhetorical purpose and audience
questions.prompt: In an 1854 speech, Frederick Douglass says the Fourth of July is a day that reveals to the slave "the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim," and adds that to him the celebration is a "sham." Which statement best identifies Douglass's purpose and its effect on his audience?
questions.answer: He turns the audience's patriotic pride against them by showing that their celebration excludes Black Americans.
choices: He turns the audience's patriotic pride against them by showing that their celebration excludes Black Americans.
He praises the holiday so warmly that his listeners forget the topic of slavery entirely.
He avoids mentioning slavery so that his audience will not feel uncomfortable or offended.
He argues that the Fourth of July should be moved to a different date on the calendar.

questions.skill: How authors define key terms
questions.prompt: In "Civil Disobedience," Henry David Thoreau writes: "The only obligation which I have a right to assume is to do at any time what I think right." How is this sentence best read as a definition within his argument?
questions.answer: He narrows the word "obligation" so that it means only a duty to one's own conscience, not to the state.
choices: He narrows the word "obligation" so that it means only a duty to one's own conscience, not to the state.
He uses "obligation" in its ordinary sense of any duty that the law places on a citizen.
He introduces the word "obligation" only to joke about it and never uses it again in the essay.
He defines "right" as a legal permission granted to citizens by the government.

questions.skill: Tracing ideas through a long text
questions.prompt: An author begins by describing one polluted river, then traces how state law, factory owners, and newspaper editors each shaped what happened to it, and ends by asking who is responsible. How does this organization serve the author's argument?
questions.answer: It moves from one concrete case to the systems behind it, so the reader sees that blame spreads across several actors.
choices: It moves from one concrete case to the systems behind it, so the reader sees that blame spreads across several actors.
It keeps the focus on a single river so that readers will not think about any larger question.
It lists unrelated examples one after another so that no cause and effect can be inferred.
It places the question at the start so that the rest of the text only repeats it without answering.

questions.skill: How authors refine a key term across a text
questions.prompt: An essay about voting rights begins: "Access to the ballot is not a favor bestowed by generous officials; it is the plainest form of consent a citizen can give." The author later returns to this idea, asking each time what "consent" requires of both the citizen and the state. How does this repetition of the key term serve the essay?
questions.answer: It lets the author steadily deepen the idea of consent from a simple privilege to a two-sided duty
choices: It lets the author steadily deepen the idea of consent from a simple privilege to a two-sided duty
It shows that the author could not think of other wording for the same idea
It signals that the essay is mainly a history of voting laws across centuries
It makes clear that consent means exactly the same thing in every part of the essay

questions.skill: Analyzing how an author rebuts a claim
questions.prompt: Read this excerpt from an essay on technology: "We are told the smartphone is a neutral tool, a simple extension of the hand. But no tool that watches its owner while it works can be called neutral." What is the main rhetorical move in the second sentence?
questions.answer: It challenges the opposing claim by offering a new definition of what makes a tool neutral
choices: It challenges the opposing claim by offering a new definition of what makes a tool neutral
It admits that the smartphone is useful and then drops the criticism entirely
It restates the first sentence in simpler words for readers who missed it
It shifts the subject from technology to a different topic altogether

titles: Concession, Qualification, and Line of Reasoning in Arguments
Evaluating the Effectiveness of an Author's Structure
The Essay as a Literary Form

questions.skill: Concession and qualification
questions.prompt: In "Politics and the English Language," George Orwell writes: "Now, it is clear that the decline of a language must have political and economic causes: it is not due simply to the bad influence of this or that individual writer." How does this concession function in his argument?
questions.answer: He grants a larger, structural cause so that his focus on individual writers' habits seems modest and harder to dismiss.
choices: He grants a larger, structural cause so that his focus on individual writers' habits seems modest and harder to dismiss.
He abandons his claim about language and admits that writing habits do not matter at all.
He argues that political causes are the only reason language ever changes over time.
He uses the concession to prove that grammar rules were invented by politicians.

questions.skill: Evaluating an argument's structure
questions.prompt: An author argues that schools should teach civics. She first states her claim, then gives three historical examples, then answers two objections, then ends with a call to action. What is the strongest judgment of this structure?
questions.answer: It builds a clear chain from claim to evidence to defense, which makes the call to action feel earned.
choices: It builds a clear chain from claim to evidence to defense, which makes the call to action feel earned.
It is weak because answering objections makes the author seem unsure of her own claim.
It is weak because the call to action comes last instead of being placed at the very start.
It works only for speeches, since readers of an essay would skip the historical examples.

questions.skill: The essay as literary form
questions.prompt: In "Self-Reliance," Ralph Waldo Emerson writes: "Society everywhere is in conspiracy against the manhood of every one of its members." He then explains what he means by this striking claim. What does this sentence show about how the personal essay works?
questions.answer: The essay lets a writer think in public, moving from a bold personal claim toward a fuller, tested idea.
choices: The essay lets a writer think in public, moving from a bold personal claim toward a fuller, tested idea.
The personal essay only reports facts and never allows the writer to state an opinion.
The sentence is a definition of "society" that Emerson applies the same way throughout all his works.
The essay form requires the writer to end every paragraph with a question for the reader.

questions.skill: Recognizing concession and its function
questions.prompt: In a book about urban life, the essayist writes: "Of course the car gave the worker freedom; no one denies the pleasure of a road that ends where he chooses. Yet that freedom quietly purchased a city where nothing essential is within walking distance." What role does the phrase "Of course" play in the argument?
questions.answer: It grants a point to the other side before the author shows its hidden cost
choices: It grants a point to the other side before the author shows its hidden cost
It introduces a claim the author believes is too obvious to need support
It signals that the author will abandon the topic of city planning entirely
It shows the author doubts the truth of everything said in the sentence

questions.skill: Evaluating whether a structure serves an essay's purpose
questions.prompt: An essayist drafts a piece about grief. He begins with the morning his father died, jumps to a story about fishing as a boy, then circles back to the funeral, and ends on the same fishing river. A peer reviewer says the essay would be stronger if it followed a clear timeline from the death to the funeral. What is the best response to this feedback?
questions.answer: The timeline order might be clearer but would strip out the essay's real subject, the way memory itself jumps between moments
choices: The timeline order might be clearer but would strip out the essay's real subject, the way memory itself jumps between moments
The reviewer is right, because no strong essay ever leaves the order of events in question
The reviewer is wrong, because personal essays should never mention events from childhood
The reviewer is right, because readers cannot follow an essay unless it ends where it begins

titles: Corroborating and Challenging Claims Across Sources

questions.skill: Weighing competing historical explanations
questions.prompt: Historians offer two explanations for the fall of Rome: one says invading armies caused it, another says internal economic decline did. A writer points out that Roman currency was debased and taxes rose for a century before the major invasions. How does this evidence affect the two explanations?
questions.answer: It supports the economic explanation by showing decline well before the invasions.
choices: It supports the economic explanation by showing decline well before the invasions.
It proves that both explanations are false and that historians know nothing about Rome.
It proves that the invading armies caused the economic problems, so only the first explanation stands.
It has no bearing, since economic facts can never be used to test a claim about military events.

questions.skill: Corroborating and challenging claims
questions.prompt: An author claims that a certain herb cures the common cold, citing a study of twenty people who took it and got better. A second source reports that in a controlled trial of two thousand people, those who took the herb recovered no faster than those who did not. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
questions.answer: The large controlled trial outweighs the small uncontrolled report, so the claim is not supported.
choices: The large controlled trial outweighs the small uncontrolled report, so the claim is not supported.
The twenty-person study is stronger because those patients actually took the herb.
Both sources must be wrong, since scientists can never agree about the common cold.
The claim is proven, because at least one study found that patients got better.

questions.skill: Literary theory approaches
questions.prompt: A student reading Plato's "Allegory of the Cave" applies formalism, historicism, and reader-response criticism. What is the key difference among these three approaches?
questions.answer: Formalism studies the text's own language and structure, historicism places it in its time, and reader-response focuses on what readers bring to it.
choices: Formalism studies the text's own language and structure, historicism places it in its time, and reader-response focuses on what readers bring to it.
All three are the same approach with different names used by different scholars.
Formalism studies the author's childhood, historicism studies the readers, and reader-response studies grammar.
Historicism ignores the past, while formalism and reader-response both focus only on the reader's feelings.

questions.skill: Testing a historical explanation against the right evidence
questions.prompt: Two sources describe a flood in 1927. Source A, a levee board memo, blames unusually heavy rain. Source B, diaries of Black sharecroppers, describes levees on their side of the river being left unrepaired while richer districts were protected. A historian argues the disaster was caused by decisions about whose land got saved. What evidence would best support the historian's claim?
questions.answer: Records showing which levee sections were repaired before the storm and which were left unfinished
choices: Records showing which levee sections were repaired before the storm and which were left unfinished
Weather records showing that the rain that year was the heaviest in decades
More diaries from residents describing how frightened they were of the water
A newspaper editorial arguing that floods are natural disasters that no one controls

questions.skill: weighing competing historical explanations
questions.prompt:
A city's newspaper was founded in 1870 and closed in 1871. Historian A argues it closed because a rival paper drew away its readers. questions.answer: Historian B's, because the mill closed a month before the last issue, while the rival only began printing after the paper had closed.

Historian A's, because the rival paper's long run shows it was strong enough to drive the first paper out of business.

Both equally, because each historian points to an event that happened in the same year as the closing.

questions.skill: Film language and camera work
questions.prompt: In a film, a character learns of her father's death while the camera slowly pulls back through a window until she is a small figure alone in a wide, empty room. What does this camera movement suggest?
questions.answer: That she is being swallowed by loneliness and isolation in the moment of her grief.
choices: That she is being swallowed by loneliness and isolation in the moment of her grief.
That the director wants to show the exact size and price of the room she is standing in.
That the scene is about to change to a different country on the next shot.

choices: That the industry claims to help ordinary people while actually crushing them.

questions.skill: Media Analysis and Film Language
questions.prompt:

What does the filmmaker achieve by carrying the father's voice over the shot of the driveway and the shot of the boy's face?

questions.skill: Previewing a textbook chapter before reading
questions.prompt: Maya is assigned a 40-page textbook chapter for Friday. Before she reads any of it, she looks at the chapter title, the section headings, the introduction, the bolded terms, and the review questions at the end. What is this step called, and why does it help?

choices: He has to read much more on his own and come to class already understanding the material.

questions.skill: Purpose of annotating and paraphrasing while reading

questions.answer: It lets him check his understanding as he reads and gives him notes to study later.

questions.answer: Reciting the section from memory to see what she retained.
choices: Reciting the section from memory to see what she retained.
Previewing the section's headings before reading it closely.
Scanning the section quickly for one single fact she needs.
Annotating the section with margin notes while she reads it.

questions.skill: Mapping a book-length argument and choosing close-reading sections

choices: Mapping the book's overall argument so he can decide what to read closely

Skipping the book and reading only a summary written by someone else
Annotating each sentence as he goes without stopping to think

questions.skill: Summarizing vs. other annotation types
questions.prompt: While reading a chapter, Lena writes in the margin: "His point here is that factory wages rose but rent rose faster." What kind of annotation is this?
questions.answer: A summary of the author's point in her own words
choices: A summary of the author's point in her own words
A question asking the author to explain something unclear
A reaction saying whether she agrees or disagrees with the point
A note connecting the chapter to something she read in another class

questions.prompt: A Renaissance poet writes of a sailor swallowed by a whale who emerges after three days, and the poem treats the event as a figure for an earlier scripture story. What is this critical device called?
questions.answer: Typology, where an Old Testament event prefigures and is fulfilled by a later one

Allegory, where each character and setting stands for an abstract moral quality throughout
Natural theology, where the design of the whale is read as evidence of a divine creator
Kenosis, where the divine is shown emptying itself into the vulnerable body of the creature

questions.skill: Ekphrasis: poetry describing visual art
questions.prompt: A poem describes a painting of a storm at sea in careful detail, then ends: "The painted wave will never break." What is this poem an example of, and what does its closing line stress?

Enjambment; the line runs on without a pause into the next

questions.prompt: A nineteenth-century poet writes a short lyric whose text was later set to music as an art song. Which account best describes what the musical setting contributes to the lyric?
questions.answer: It imposes a musical phrase and breath structure that reshapes the poem's pacing and emphasis, so the sung version's form is a property of the setting and not simply of the printed text.

It simply duplicates the poem's printed meter in musical time, so the song adds no formal structure beyond what the page already gives.

questions.skill: Memory, trauma, and testimony in literature
questions.prompt: A novel tells the story of a genocide through a witness who says again and again, "I remember, but I cannot make you understand." Critics describe the book as bearing witness to an event that resists full telling. What key idea does this describe?

Allegory: each character stands for a moral virtue

questions.prompt: William Morris's News from Nowhere (1890) was written as an answer to Edward Bellamy's Looking Backward (1888). questions.prompt: A novelist writes: "My grandmother fled Warsaw in 1943. I was born in 1971 and was never there, but the photographs on her mantel and the stories she told at night are the truest things I know. Collective memory, a shared group recollection that shapes a community's identity over time

questions.skill: Identifying gaps in scholarship
questions.prompt: A doctoral student is reading an article and wants to identify what it leaves unaddressed. Which reading question targets a GAPS analysis rather than argument or method?
questions.answer: What evidence or cases does the study not examine, and which questions does the author explicitly set aside?
choices: What evidence or cases does the study not examine, and which questions does the author explicitly set aside?
What is the author's central claim, and how does each section build toward it?
How was the study's evidence gathered, and what are the limits of that procedure?
How does this article's claim revise or challenge the earlier work it cites?

questions.skill: Reading scholarship in a research language
questions.prompt: A graduate student must satisfy a research language requirement by reading scholarship in French. Which plan uses the second scholarly language in the way the requirement is meant to test?
questions.answer: Read an entire French scholarly monograph relevant to the dissertation and summarize its argument and evidence in notes.
choices: Read an entire French scholarly monograph relevant to the dissertation and summarize its argument and evidence in notes.
Use a translation app to render a French article into English word by word, then file the English text.
Memorize a list of French literary terms and vocabulary with no reading of actual scholarship.
Read only the English abstract and the bibliography of a French article, skipping the body.

questions.skill: Synthesizing scholarly reading with notes
questions.prompt: A student must keep track of about two hundred sources for a literature review. Which note-taking practice best supports synthesizing that scholarship later?
questions.answer: Record, for each source, the thesis, the method, the evidence, and a note on how it relates to two or three other sources read so far.
choices: Record, for each source, the thesis, the method, the evidence, and a note on how it relates to two or three other sources read so far.
Copy several pages of each source verbatim into one large document, in the order the sources are read.
Save each source in the reference manager with its citation data but write no notes on content.
Write a one-word reaction to each source, such as 'useful' or 'old,' and move on to the next.

questions.skill: Identifying the central argument of a scholarly article
questions.prompt: A graduate student reads a scholarly article and needs to state its central claim as the author frames it. Which question targets the article's ARGUMENT?
questions.answer: What conclusion does the author draw from the evidence, and how do the section headings lead to it?
choices: What conclusion does the author draw from the evidence, and how do the section headings lead to it?
What earlier scholarship on this topic does the author cite in the literature review?
Which archives and databases did the author search to assemble the corpus?
Which related topics does the author explicitly leave for future research?

questions.skill: Evaluating the research method of a scholarly book
questions.prompt: A doctoral student must evaluate a book's method before citing it. Which question assesses the METHOD rather than the argument or the gaps?
questions.answer: How were the primary texts selected, and what does that selection let the author claim?
choices: How were the primary texts selected, and what does that selection let the author claim?
What is the author's main claim about the relationship between the two genres?
Which scholars does the author disagree with most directly in the introduction?
What follow-up study would build on this book's findings?

questions.skill: Critiquing a theoretical application
questions.prompt: A student applies a psychoanalytic reading to a novel and treats the characters as patients whose desires can be diagnosed. Which habit makes this use of theory weakest as literary scholarship?
questions.answer: It treats fictional characters as clinical cases and skips how the text's form, language, and narration shape desire.
choices: It treats fictional characters as clinical cases and skips how the text's form, language, and narration shape desire.
It draws on a theoretical school developed in a field other than literary studies.
It focuses on desire and conflict rather than on the author's stated intentions.
It compares the novel with other novels written in the same period.

questions.skill: Medieval genre and scholarship
questions.prompt: A student argues that a medieval dream vision, in which the narrator falls asleep and meets allegorical figures, is best read through a feminist lens on the female voice. Which approach fits the text's own medieval literary conventions?
questions.answer: Reading the dream vision as a genre with established conventions, then asking how the poem's use of the female dreamer speaks back to them.
choices: Reading the dream vision as a genre with established conventions, then asking how the poem's use of the female dreamer speaks back to them.
Judging the poem by how closely its plot follows a real medieval woman's life story.
Treating the allegorical figures as flat characters and measuring them against modern psychological realism.
Ignoring the dream framework because the poem's historical facts are what matter most.

questions.skill: Early modern rhetorical conventions
questions.prompt: A student reads a seventeenth-century prose text in which the speaker presents an argument as a series of imagined objections and replies. Which description identifies the device most useful for reading early modern argumentative prose?
questions.answer: A dialogic or controversia-like structure in which the speaker stages counterarguments before answering them.
choices: A dialogic or controversia-like structure in which the speaker stages counterarguments before answering them.
A lyric apostrophe in which the speaker addresses an absent beloved throughout the passage.
An epic simile that compares the speaker's situation at length to a scene from classical myth.
A pastoral eclogue in which two shepherds debate in a rural setting using conventional imagery.

questions.skill: Applying a theoretical school's key concept to formal features of a text
questions.prompt: A student applies Bakhtin's concept of heteroglossia, developed in his essays on the novel, to a nineteenth-century novel in which several social voices and dialects compete within the narration. Which question follows from treating heteroglossia as a formal property of the novel rather than as a theme?
questions.answer: How does the narration stage competing social languages within the prose itself, rather than merely reporting that characters speak in dialect?
choices: How does the narration stage competing social languages within the prose itself, rather than merely reporting that characters speak in dialect?
Does the novel express Bakhtin's own political views about the Russian peasantry?
Which characters in the novel best represent the ideals of the community?
Does the novel show that one social class is more virtuous than the others?

questions.skill: Understanding how literary scholarship and its methods have changed over time
questions.prompt: A student is tracing how the study of Renaissance literature changed across the twentieth century. Which question belongs to the history of the discipline rather than to a single reading of a play?
questions.answer: How did the rise of New Criticism in the mid-twentieth century shift attention from an author's biography to the verbal structure of the text?
choices: How did the rise of New Criticism in the mid-twentieth century shift attention from an author's biography to the verbal structure of the text?
What does the imagery of disease in this particular tragedy suggest about the city it depicts?
Which sources did this playwright draw on when writing the plot of this play?
How does the soliloquy in this scene reveal the speaker's state of mind?

questions.skill: Romantic lyric and landscape
questions.prompt: A student reads an early nineteenth-century lyric in which a ruined abbey, wild mountains, and the passing of time stir the speaker's solitary reflections. Which reading of the passage fits the period's characteristic concerns?
questions.answer: It joins landscape and ruin to the speaker's inward feeling, a hallmark of Romantic lyric practice.
choices: It joins landscape and ruin to the speaker's inward feeling, a hallmark of Romantic lyric practice.
It uses the ruined abbey chiefly as a puzzle to be solved with documentary evidence from the local parish records.
It presents the landscape as a problem to be managed by urban planning and civic improvement.
It keeps the speaker's feelings in the background so that the reader's attention stays on public debate.

questions.skill: Victorian science and culture
questions.prompt: A student reads an 1859 essay that argues natural selection explains how species change over time, and that the process follows from struggle and inheritance in large populations. Which context best explains the essay's importance for Victorian literature and culture?
questions.answer: It unsettled natural theology and fixed species, feeding Victorian debates about design, progress, and humanity's place in nature.
choices: It unsettled natural theology and fixed species, feeding Victorian debates about design, progress, and humanity's place in nature.
It settled the question of species by showing that all living forms were created separately and unchanged.
It was a technical treatise on steam engines that had no effect on Victorian writing or thought.
It argued that human societies evolve in fixed stages, a claim later Victorian novelists adopted unchanged.

questions.skill: Modernist form
questions.prompt: A student reads an early twentieth-century novel in which the story moves through the shifting impressions and memories of several minds in a single city day, with little conventional plot. Which feature best identifies the work as modernist?
questions.answer: Its use of fragmented perspective and stream of consciousness to render inner life rather than a stable chronological plot.
choices: Its use of fragmented perspective and stream of consciousness to render inner life rather than a stable chronological plot.
Its use of a reliable omniscient narrator who judges each character's morality for the reader.
Its use of a plain chronological plot that follows one hero from birth to death in clear stages.
Its use of direct dialogue and stage-like scenes with no attention to inner thought.

questions.skill: Placing postwar British fiction in its social and historical context
questions.prompt: A student reads a 1950s British novel in which a young man from a working-class background voices anger at the university, the church, and the class system that has shaped his life. Which reading best fits the postwar context in which the novel appeared?
questions.answer: The novel belongs to a postwar current of writing that gave voice to class resentment after the expansion of higher education and the welfare state.
choices: The novel belongs to a postwar current of writing that gave voice to class resentment after the expansion of higher education and the welfare state.
The novel anticipates the Romantic celebration of individual feeling against industrial society.

questions.skill: Recognizing postmodern features of late twentieth-century American literature
questions.prompt: A student reads a late twentieth-century American novel that mixes advertising slogans, popular song lyrics, and abrupt shifts between genres while questioning whether coherent characters and stable meanings are possible. Which context best explains the features of this novel?
questions.answer: Postmodern American fiction of the late twentieth century, which absorbed mass culture and questioned stable meaning and unified character.
choices: Postmodern American fiction of the late twentieth century, which absorbed mass culture and questioned stable meaning and unified character.
American modernism of the 1920s, which sought to represent the nation through epic form and myth.

questions.skill: Postcolonial reading
questions.prompt: A student reads a twentieth-century novel in English by a writer from a formerly colonized country, in which a young man from a village travels to the colonial capital and finds himself divided between local speech and the colonizer's tongue. questions.skill: Comparative method
questions.prompt: A student compares a Chinese classical poem with a poem written in English four centuries later, without reading Chinese. Which practice makes the comparison methodologically responsible?
questions.answer: Acknowledging that the Chinese poem is accessed through translation, and asking how the translators' choices shape what is compared.
choices: Acknowledging that the Chinese poem is accessed through translation, and asking how the translators' choices shape what is compared.
Treating the English translation as identical to the Chinese original in every respect.
Comparing only the poems' themes and ignoring language, form, and historical context.

questions.skill: Translation and reception
questions.prompt: A student studies a novel that was largely forgotten until a new English translation made it a celebrated work a century after its first publication. Which claim about translation and reception is best supported by this case?

choices: Translation can reshape a work's reputation, since a new version can bring a text to readers and critics who could not read the original.

questions.skill: Reading literature through the history of gender and sexuality
questions.prompt: A student reads an eighteenth-century novel in which a young woman must choose a husband and her fortune depends on the choice, and the narration marks the limited options available to women of her class. questions.skill: Reading translated works alongside originals to see what translation shapes
questions.prompt: A student reads an English translation of a novel from the Japanese and notices that the translation renders a range of politeness levels and honorifics into plain English prose. What does this observation suggest about the translation?

questions.skill: Race and identity in literature
questions.prompt: A student reads an 1899 novella in which a Creole woman in New Orleans feels confined by marriage and the expectations placed on women of her class. Which question belongs to a seminar on race, ethnicity, and identity?

questions.skill: Genre history and theory
questions.prompt: A student is studying the sonnet as a genre across periods. Which question follows from treating the sonnet as a genre with a history?

choices: How do later poets work with and against the fourteen-line form and its established conventions of turn and couplet?

questions.skill: Poetic form and poetics
questions.prompt: A student reads a short poem that claims, in the first person, 'I celebrate myself, and sing myself,' published in 1855. Which approach shows advanced attention to poetic form?
questions.answer: Asking how the poem's long, catalog-like lines and free verse build a speaking self, and how that form departs from regular meter and rhyme.
choices: Asking how the poem's long, catalog-like lines and free verse build a speaking self, and how that form departs from regular meter and rhyme.
Counting only the number of lines in the poem and reporting that number as the poem's form.

questions.skill: Reading dramatic texts through their performance history
questions.prompt: A student studies a printed play script and notices that the same scene is staged very differently in three modern productions: one uses a bare stage, one a realistic nineteenth-century drawing room, and one a contemporary office. choices: How does each staging's choice of setting and design shape the audience's understanding of the play's conflict?

questions.skill: Studying a genre's conventions, history, and theory
questions.prompt: A student is writing about how the elegy, a poem of mourning, has been written from ancient Greece to the present. Which approach treats the elegy as a genre with a history and theory rather than as a label for any sad poem?

choices: Tracing how elegiac conventions, such as lament and consolation, are revised or resisted by poets in different periods.

Ranking elegies by the fame of the poets who wrote them.
Focusing only on the personal grief the poet experienced while writing.

questions.skill: Author studies and reception

Reading only the most famous novel and treating it as a summary of everything the author wrote.

questions.skill: Literature across media

questions.skill: Critiquing empirical research on how readers process literature

questions.prompt: A student is studying a nineteenth-century novel as it was first published: in monthly installments in a magazine, with advertisements and illustrations surrounding each installment. Which question belongs to literature and media rather than to a reading of the novel's plot alone?

questions.skill: Book format and collation (descriptive bibliography)

questions.skill: Analyzing film sound: diegetic and non-diegetic
questions.prompt: In a film, a jazz trio plays in a café and the characters at the table turn to look at the band. When the scene cuts to a bus at night, the same tune keeps playing, though no one on the bus reacts to it. How is the music best described in the two parts of the film?
questions.answer: Diegetic in the café, where it has a source inside the story world, and non-diegetic over the bus scene, where it has none.

questions.skill: Reading manuscript abbreviations (paleography)

choices: Both are abbreviations: the letter y is written for the old letter thorn (þ) in the word "the," and the mark is the Tironian sign that stands for "and."

questions.skill: Reading paper structure and watermarks in descriptive bibliography
questions.prompt: A descriptive bibliographer examines a hand-press book and finds that the printed pages carry a faint pattern of horizontal lines spaced about two centimeters apart, with a small crest visible in one corner of a sheet. What does this evidence tell her about the book's paper?
questions.answer: It is laid paper, made on a wire sieve, and the crest is a watermark identifying the papermaker or mill.

The lines are ruling drawn by a scribe before printing, and the crest is the library mark of an early owner.

questions.skill: Analyzing sound bridges and the source of film sound
questions.prompt: In a film, a factory whistle blows and the workers on the line look up as the shift ends. A moment later the shot changes to a woman waiting at a window in a different city, and the sound of the whistle continues over her shot as well. How is the whistle sound used here?

choices: It is sound from the factory scene whose source is on screen there, carried over the next shot as a sound bridge linking the two scenes.
It is a score element added by the director to build mood, with no source anywhere in the story world.
It is dubbed dialogue recorded after shooting to correct the workers' voices in the factory scene.

questions.skill: Encoding variants in TEI XML
questions.prompt: In a TEI XML edition, a place where the manuscripts disagree is encoded as: <app><lem>floures</lem><rdg wit="#A">floures</rdg><rdg wit="#B">flowres</rdg></app>. What does this encoding record?
questions.answer: An apparatus of variant readings at this word, with the reading the editor prints marked as the lemma and each other reading linked to the manuscript that has it.
choices: An apparatus of variant readings at this word, with the reading the editor prints marked as the lemma and each other reading linked to the manuscript that has it.
The structure of the poem at this point, marking the word as the end of a line and the end of a stanza in the manuscript.
The editors' regularized spelling, marking the original form of the word in the manuscript and the form used in the edited text.
The page layout of the copy-text, marking where a page break falls at this word and how the word was hyphenated there.

questions.skill: Copy-text and emendation (textual editing)
questions.prompt: An editor of a play works from two quartos, Q1 (1604) and Q2 (1611). The two differ in punctuation, spelling, and a few words. She keeps Q1's punctuation and spelling throughout, but where Q1's word makes nonsense she prints the reading of Q2. What editorial principle is she following?
questions.answer: Copy-text editing: Q1 serves as the copy-text for accidentals, while substantive readings are emended from other witnesses where the copy-text is in error.
choices: Copy-text editing: Q1 serves as the copy-text for accidentals, while substantive readings are emended from other witnesses where the copy-text is in error.
Best-text editing: the earliest witness is printed exactly as it stands, and no reading is ever taken from a later witness.
Stemmatic editing: the readings of all surviving copies are arranged in a family tree to reconstruct the lost archetype.
Social-text editing: the play is presented as the work of a group of collaborators, and the readings of every witness are printed in parallel.

questions.skill: Illumination and manuscript decoration (codicology)
questions.prompt: At the start of a psalm in a manuscript, the large opening letter "D" contains a small painted scene of a king playing a harp, on a gold background. What is this feature called, and how is it read?

choices: A historiated initial: the picture inside the letter illustrates or names the subject of the text that begins here.
A decorated initial: the ornament inside the letter is abstract, and the scene bears no relation to the written text.
A miniature: an independent picture placed before the text, with no connection to the letter that opens it.
A bas-de-page drawing: a scene painted at the foot of the page and read apart from the text above it.

questions.skill: Describing gatherings and quires in codicology
questions.prompt: A codicologist turns through a handwritten book and notices that most of the units of leaves sewn together are made of four sheets folded once, giving eight leaves, but two units are made of a single folded sheet, giving two leaves. How should she describe the book's structure?
questions.answer: Its gatherings are mostly quaternions, with two gatherings of one folded sheet, so a collation formula would record that mixture.
choices: Its gatherings are mostly quaternions, with two gatherings of one folded sheet, so a collation formula would record that mixture.
Its gatherings are all of four sheets folded twice, so the book is uniformly quarto in structure.

questions.skill: Reading provenance evidence to trace ownership history

choices: The book was given by its author to a reader named E. Browne in 1671, and the inscriptions are provenance evidence tracing early ownership.

questions.skill: Stylometric distance (Burrows's Delta)

questions.skill: Planning a second book project
questions.prompt: A scholar finishing her first monograph is choosing her second book project. Which plan best follows the standard advice for a second book?
questions.answer: Developing a new major project that shows a distinct research program beyond the dissertation-derived first book.
choices: Developing a new major project that shows a distinct research program beyond the dissertation-derived first book.
Turning the dissertation into a revised second edition, since the first book was published too quickly.
Collecting eight previously published articles into a single volume to demonstrate productivity before tenure review.
Writing a short polemic on the field's current debates so the second book can appear within a year of the first.

questions.skill: Establishing a copy-text for a scholarly edition
questions.prompt: An editor is preparing a scholarly edition of a 19th-century novel that survives in a manuscript draft, a first edition, and an author-revised printing. What is the essential first decision of scholarly editing?
questions.answer: Choosing the copy-text — which version supplies the base wording — and stating the editorial rationale for that choice.
choices: Choosing the copy-text — which version supplies the base wording — and stating the editorial rationale for that choice.
Choosing the cheapest version to typeset, since the wording of all versions is identical in every respect.
Printing all three versions in full, one after another, so that readers can compare them without editorial guidance.
Silently modernizing spelling and punctuation in all versions to make the text easier for today's students to read.

questions.skill: Curating contributions for an edited collection
questions.prompt: An editor has commissioned ten essays for a collection and received a strong paper that does not fit the volume's stated thesis. What is the soundest editorial action?
questions.answer: Either declining the essay with a clear explanation of the fit problem or renegotiating the volume's framing with all contributors.
choices: Either declining the essay with a clear explanation of the fit problem or renegotiating the volume's framing with all contributors.
Accepting the essay as is and quietly removing the volume's thesis from the introduction.
Accepting the essay but adding a footnote admitting that it does not belong in the collection.
Asking the author to add two paragraphs citing the other contributors so the paper appears thematically linked.

questions.skill: Choosing a viable second book project
questions.prompt: A scholar's first book grew out of her dissertation. For her second book, she is weighing two options: (A) a new monograph on a different period and method, requiring several years of new archival research, or (B) a monograph that reworks and expands five of her already-published articles on the first book's topic into a single argument. Which plan best follows standard advice for a second book project?
questions.answer: Option A, because a second book should establish an independent research program rather than consolidate existing work.
choices: Option A, because a second book should establish an independent research program rather than consolidate existing work.
Option B, because reworking published articles is the fastest route to a second book and tenure committees value speed.
Option B, because a second book is expected to extend the dissertation's argument in a single sustained form.
Option A, because second books are expected to be edited collections rather than solo monographs, so a new topic is required.

questions.skill: Enforcing coherence across commissioned essays
questions.prompt: An editor has commissioned fifteen essays for a collection and has received the full set of drafts. Several contributors define the volume's key term differently, and two essays cite the same primary source with conflicting publication dates. What is the soundest editorial action at this stage?
questions.answer: Write a shared introduction that defines the key term and sets citation and bibliographic standards, then ask contributors to revise to those standards.
choices: Write a shared introduction that defines the key term and sets citation and bibliographic standards, then ask contributors to revise to those standards.
Publish the essays as submitted, since contributors retain authority over their own arguments and definitions.
Remove the key term from the volume's title so that differing definitions no longer create a problem.
Rewrite the offending passages yourself without consulting contributors, since the editor has final responsibility for consistency.

titles: [All Tracks] Reading and Reviewing Manuscripts for Journals and Presses

questions.skill: Writing overview essays for handbooks
questions.prompt: A contributor to a major handbook must survey an entire subfield in 5,000 words. What should the essay prioritize?
questions.answer: A balanced overview of the subfield's main problems, debates, and landmark works, written for readers who are not specialists in it.
choices: A balanced overview of the subfield's main problems, debates, and landmark works, written for readers who are not specialists in it.
A detailed defense of the author's own latest article, since the handbook slot is a chance to advance a personal argument.
A complete annotated bibliography listing every publication in the subfield from the past fifty years.
A polemic advocating one side of the subfield's central controversy, since handbook essays should take firm positions.

questions.skill: Fair and ethical peer review
questions.prompt: A peer reviewer finds a manuscript whose central claim she has also argued in an unpublished paper of her own. What is the correct procedure?
questions.answer: Declare the competing interest to the editor and, if asked to review, evaluate only the manuscript's arguments without exploiting the privileged access.
choices: Declare the competing interest to the editor and, if asked to review, evaluate only the manuscript's arguments without exploiting the privileged access.
Speed her own paper to publication first, since the manuscript is not yet published and establishes no priority.
Recommend rejection in the report without mentioning the overlap, letting the editor draw the conclusion.
Copy the manuscript's useful evidence into her own paper, since peer review gives her lawful access to the material.

questions.skill: Critically evaluating computational scholarship
questions.prompt: A published digital humanities study claims its model classifies periodical essays by political affiliation with 95% accuracy, but the training and test essays share authors. What is the key critical point?
questions.answer: The evaluation likely leaks authorial signal into both sets, so the accuracy may reflect authorship rather than political stance.
choices: The evaluation likely leaks authorial signal into both sets, so the accuracy may reflect authorship rather than political stance.
A 95% accuracy rate is too low to publish in the humanities, where results should be at least 99% accurate.
The study is invalid because machine learning can never be applied to political texts of any kind.
The model should be rejected because training data and test data must always come from different centuries.

questions.skill: Structuring a peer review report
questions.prompt: A peer reviewer has finished reading a manuscript and must write her report. The manuscript's central argument is original and persuasive, but its literature review omits three major studies from the past five years, and one figure is mislabeled. What is the soundest structure for her report?
questions.answer: Separate the major issue (the outdated literature review) from the minor ones (the mislabeled figure), and explain clearly what revision would resolve each.
choices: Separate the major issue (the outdated literature review) from the minor ones (the mislabeled figure), and explain clearly what revision would resolve each.
Lead with the mislabeled figure to build goodwill, then mention the missing studies briefly at the end of the report.
Recommend rejection, since an incomplete literature review means the manuscript cannot be trusted at all.
List every problem in the order encountered while reading, without distinguishing which issues affect the argument.

questions.skill: Critically evaluating data and methods in DH scholarship
questions.prompt: A published digital humanities article argues that a set of word-embedding models reveals changing concepts of 'nature' in nineteenth-century poetry, using a corpus of 200 poems. The article reports no information about which editions the poems were taken from or how the corpus was selected. What is the most important critical question for a reader evaluating this claim?
questions.answer: Whether the corpus selection and source editions are documented well enough for the result to be reproduced and checked.
choices: Whether the corpus selection and source editions are documented well enough for the result to be reproduced and checked.
Whether word embeddings are a legitimate method for literary study at all, since they were developed for computer science.
Whether 200 poems is a large enough number for any statistical claim to be meaningful.
Whether the article's author has published other work on nineteenth-century poetry before.

questions.skill: Building and documenting a research corpus
questions.prompt: A researcher assembles a corpus of 19th-century periodicals and plans to share it. Which practice is essential for corpus curation?
questions.answer: Documenting selection criteria, provenance, and encoding decisions in a README or metadata schema so others can assess and reuse the corpus.
choices: Documenting selection criteria, provenance, and encoding decisions in a README or metadata schema so others can assess and reuse the corpus.
Keeping the selection criteria private so that competing labs cannot reproduce the same corpus.
Including every digitized text found, since corpus quality always improves with more documents.
Converting all texts to image-only PDFs so that the original page layouts are preserved exactly.

questions.skill: Tracking emerging scholarship
questions.prompt: A scholar wants to keep up with new work in her field across journals, conferences, and preprints. Which approach is most effective and sustainable?
questions.answer: Setting up systematic alerts and feeds for key journals, repositories, and conferences, with a regular scheduled time to triage the results.
choices: Setting up systematic alerts and feeds for key journals, repositories, and conferences, with a regular scheduled time to triage the results.
Reading each new issue of the top journal cover to cover once a year during the summer break.
Depending on colleagues to mention anything important, since curated word of mouth is the most reliable filter.
Searching each database from scratch whenever a paper is being written, since alerts mostly produce clutter.

questions.skill: Leading multi-site reading research
questions.prompt: A research team is running a reading intervention study across four schools with different curricula. What is the most important design step before launching?
questions.answer: Standardizing the intervention protocol and fidelity measures across sites while allowing documented site-level adaptations.
choices: Standardizing the intervention protocol and fidelity measures across sites while allowing documented site-level adaptations.
Letting each site design its own version of the intervention so that results reflect real classroom diversity.
Running all four schools at once with no training for site staff, to keep the study as naturalistic as possible.
Analyzing each site's results separately and reporting only the site with the strongest effect.

questions.skill: Documenting and versioning a shared corpus
questions.prompt: A research team has assembled a shared corpus of early twentieth-century newspaper articles and wants other scholars to reuse it. A year after the first release, the team corrects OCR errors in several thousand articles and adds new metadata fields. What is the essential practice for curating this corpus over time?
questions.answer: Version each release, document what changed between versions, and keep earlier versions accessible so prior studies can be verified.
choices: Version each release, document what changed between versions, and keep earlier versions accessible so prior studies can be verified.
Replace the earlier files in place, so that users always work from the most accurate version available.
Release the corrected corpus only to collaborators, since public releases should never contain known errors.
Add the corrections without documentation, since the changes improve accuracy and do not need explanation.

questions.skill: Balancing preprints and peer-reviewed sources when tracking a field
questions.prompt: A scholar wants to track emerging work in her field. She hears that a preprint server in her discipline now posts papers months before journal publication, but she knows that preprints have not yet been peer reviewed. How should she incorporate preprints into her tracking practice?
questions.answer: Monitor preprints to learn about new work early, but treat their findings as provisional until they pass peer review, and note their status when citing them.
choices: Monitor preprints to learn about new work early, but treat their findings as provisional until they pass peer review, and note their status when citing them.
Ignore preprints entirely, since only peer-reviewed journal articles count as scholarship in the field.
Cite preprints as equivalent to published articles, since their content is usually unchanged by the review process.
Wait until a preprint is published before reading it, since reading unreviewed work wastes time.

questions.skill: Conducting meta-analysis of reading research
questions.prompt: A meta-analysis of a reading intervention reports a large average effect, but the included studies differ sharply in outcome measures and populations. What is the strongest next step?
questions.answer: Run moderator analyses and inspect heterogeneity (e.g., I²) to determine which study features account for the variation.
choices: Run moderator analyses and inspect heterogeneity (e.g., I²) to determine which study features account for the variation.
Report only the average effect size, since averaging removes the influence of differences among studies.
Exclude the most unusual studies so that the remaining results appear more consistent.
Convert all effect sizes to the same metric, which by itself eliminates the heterogeneity.

questions.skill: Translating research into practice
questions.prompt: A state agency asks a researcher to turn a set of decoding-intervention findings into classroom guidance. Which step best supports sound translation?
questions.answer: Specifying the conditions and populations where the evidence holds, and stating uncertainty where evidence is thin.
choices: Specifying the conditions and populations where the evidence holds, and stating uncertainty where evidence is thin.
Presenting the findings as universal laws of reading that apply to every grade and learner without exception.
Leaving out effect sizes and study limitations so that the guidance is brief and easy for teachers to read.
Waiting for perfect evidence before issuing any guidance, even if districts need direction this year.

questions.skill: Implementation science for literacy programs

questions.answer: An implementation study measuring fidelity, context, and local capacity at both pilot and scale-up sites.
choices: An implementation study measuring fidelity, context, and local capacity at both pilot and scale-up sites.
A replication of the original efficacy trial in one pilot district, this time with a larger sample.
A survey asking teachers only whether they liked the program, since satisfaction predicts outcomes.
A policy analysis of state funding formulas that ignores what happened inside the classrooms.

questions.skill: Interpreting heterogeneous outcomes in a meta-analysis
questions.prompt: A systematic review synthesizes twelve studies of a vocabulary intervention. The studies report outcomes on different measures: some use standardized reading tests, others use researcher-designed vocabulary quizzes, and sample sizes range from 30 to 900 students. The review reports a single average effect size across all twelve studies. What is the most important caution about this average?
questions.answer: Because the outcome measures and sample sizes differ substantially, the single average may obscure meaningful differences and should be interpreted alongside those differences.
choices: Because the outcome measures and sample sizes differ substantially, the single average may obscure meaningful differences and should be interpreted alongside those differences.
The average is reliable as long as all twelve studies used random assignment, regardless of their outcome measures.
The average is invalid, since effect sizes cannot be computed across studies with different sample sizes.
The average should be weighted by publication date, since more recent studies are always more reliable.

questions.skill: Studying implementation fidelity and adaptation
questions.prompt: A well-validated literacy program is being adopted in a new district. Fidelity data show that teachers are implementing only about half the prescribed lesson components, but reading gains in the district are close to those found in the original trials. A researcher is asked to explain this result. What is the most important next step in studying it?
questions.answer: Examine which components teachers are actually using and whether the adaptations they have made preserve the program's active ingredients.
choices: Examine which components teachers are actually using and whether the adaptations they have made preserve the program's active ingredients.
Conclude that the program does not work, since low fidelity automatically invalidates any observed gains.
Conclude that fidelity does not matter, since outcomes were similar despite low implementation.
Increase monitoring of fidelity without investigating the teachers' adaptations, since fidelity is the only relevant measure.

titles: [Literature] Comparative Poetics and Non-Western Reading Traditions

questions.skill: Applying copy-text theory to editorial practice
questions.prompt: An editor of a twentieth-century novel adopts the first edition's spelling and punctuation throughout, but where a later edition authorized by the author carries wording that the editor judges better, the editor prints the later wording and records the change in an editorial note. Which editorial principle does this practice follow?
questions.answer: W. W. Greg's copy-text rationale: one witness governs the accidentals, while substantive readings are chosen from any witness on their merits.
choices: W. W. Greg's copy-text rationale: one witness governs the accidentals, while substantive readings are chosen from any witness on their merits.
The principle of final authorial intention: the last version authorized by the author should be reproduced whole, for both wording and accidentals.
Jerome McGann's social-text principle: every version is a complete social product and should be reproduced without emendation.
The versioning principle: all variant forms should be printed in parallel columns, because no single form can claim authority.

questions.skill: Distinguishing genuine period concepts from over-broad period labels
questions.prompt: A literary historian argues that "Romanticism" names several distinct movements — one centering on the organic and the picturesque, another on the heroic and the sublime, a third on the plain style of political dissent — and that writers conventionally placed in the period belong to only one or two of them. What follows for the way literary history should be written?
questions.answer: A period label should be defined by the specific traits its writers share, not by a single abstraction that covers several distinct movements.
choices: A period label should be defined by the specific traits its writers share, not by a single abstraction that covers several distinct movements.
The several movements should be arranged as sequential stages of one Romanticism, each beginning where the previous one ends.
The period should be dated by the political events of the age, since only a political boundary can separate literary movements reliably.
Since the term covers several movements, it should be replaced by the name of the one movement with the most adherents.

questions.skill: Using non-Western poetics to challenge Western theoretical categories
questions.prompt: Earl Miner's Comparative Poetics observes that Japanese poetic theory grew out of lyric poetry and personal expression, while Western poetic theory grew out of public, mimetic kinds such as epic and drama. A scholar proposes to write a comparative poetics that begins by defining literature as three kinds — epic, lyric, and drama — and then describes how the Japanese tradition fills each slot. What is the main problem with this plan?
questions.answer: It makes the Western scheme the neutral frame, so the Japanese tradition will be described by what it lacks instead of by what it organizes itself around.
choices: It makes the Western scheme the neutral frame, so the Japanese tradition will be described by what it lacks instead of by what it organizes itself around.
It assumes that Japanese literature contains no poetry, when in fact poetry is the oldest Japanese form.
It relies on Miner's account, which has been discredited by scholars who found mistranslations of Aristotle in it.
It assumes the two traditions value the three kinds equally, when Western poetics has always ranked the lyric highest.

questions.skill: Choosing among copy-texts in a critical edition
questions.prompt: A scholar prepares a critical edition of a seventeenth-century poet whose poems circulated for decades in handwritten copies before any printed book appeared. Each surviving copy differs from the others in wording. Which principle should guide the choice of a copy-text?
questions.answer: Select as copy-text the copy whose wording best fits the poet's habits of composition as evidenced across all surviving copies.
choices: Select as copy-text the copy whose wording best fits the poet's habits of composition as evidenced across all surviving copies.
Use the earliest surviving handwritten copy as copy-text and reproduce its wording exactly throughout.
Print the wording found in the majority of surviving copies and treat majority agreement as authorial.
Follow the first printed edition, since printing marks the point at which the poems became a fixed text.

questions.skill: Evaluating a new periodization of literary history
questions.prompt: A literary historian proposes a new account of the novel: rather than the usual split between "the eighteenth-century novel" and "the nineteenth-century novel," the historian groups works by the publishing market that produced them — circulating-library fiction, serial magazine fiction, and single-volume fiction. What is the main scholarly risk of this proposal?
questions.answer: It may sort works by the circumstances of their sale rather than by features of the writing itself.
choices: It may sort works by the circumstances of their sale rather than by features of the writing itself.
It relies on market records that have not survived for most novels of the period.
It assumes that novels were written for readers in a single country rather than for export.

titles: [All Tracks] Field-Defining Reviews and State-of-the-Field Essays

questions.skill: Recognizing what makes an author study field-reshaping
questions.prompt: Two scholars publish book-length studies of the same novelist. The first assembles previously uncollected letters and corrects the chronology of composition. The second argues that the novelist's apparent realism is a deliberate critique of the realist form itself, and that reading the novels this way resolves the disagreements that had split the field. Which description best distinguishes the second study's contribution?
questions.answer: It reorganizes the field's disagreements around a new governing claim about the whole body of work.
choices: It reorganizes the field's disagreements around a new governing claim about the whole body of work.
It supplies new primary evidence, which is the only way an author study can change how a field reads the work.
It gathers the existing criticism into one place so that later scholars can see the full range of readings already available.
It places the novelist inside a new period scheme, so that the period rather than the author becomes the unit of analysis.

questions.skill: Identifying the characteristic moves of a state-of-the-field essay
questions.prompt: A senior scholar is invited to write a state-of-the-field essay covering twenty years of scholarship on a major poet. Which set of moves would make the essay field-defining rather than merely bibliographic?
questions.answer: Naming the assumption that has organized most of the work, showing where following it has stopped yielding results, and proposing a question the field has not asked.
choices: Naming the assumption that has organized most of the work, showing where following it has stopped yielding results, and proposing a question the field has not asked.
Listing the books and articles published in the period with a one-sentence summary of each, and noting which are most frequently cited.
Defending the scholar's own earlier reading of the poet against the interpretations published in the years since.
Comparing how the poet has been read in several countries and ranking the national traditions by the quality of their criticism.

questions.skill: Judging a field's evidence base and naming what is missing
questions.prompt: In a survey of twenty years of scholarship, a critic writes: "Almost every study of this poet's late work has relied on the same three letters as evidence of the poet's state of mind. No study has examined the drafts that survive in the poet's notebooks." What is this passage doing for the field?
questions.answer: Identifying the evidentiary base the field has shared and the archive it has left out, which sets up a research agenda.
choices: Identifying the evidentiary base the field has shared and the archive it has left out, which sets up a research agenda.
Arguing that the three letters are forgeries and that every study built on them must be discarded.
Recommending that the late work be dropped from the canon until stronger evidence about the poet's state of mind exists.
Summarizing the contents of the three letters so that readers of the survey need not consult them.

questions.skill: Judging evidence about authorial intention in author studies
questions.prompt: A scholar writes a study of a major novelist that many reviewers expect to settle the debate about the novelist's intentions. The scholar's central argument is that the novelist's letters show a deliberate plan for each novel. What is the most important objection a rival scholar would raise?
questions.answer: Letters may reflect the self-image the novelist wanted to present, not the working intentions behind the fiction.
choices: Letters may reflect the self-image the novelist wanted to present, not the working intentions behind the fiction.
The novelist's letters are already well known and have been quoted in earlier studies.
A single scholar cannot establish an author's intentions without a full archival team.
Novelists rarely plan their works in advance, so letters about plans prove nothing.

questions.skill: Distinguishing field-defining essays from bibliographic surveys
questions.prompt: A journal editor receives a state-of-the-field essay on a century of scholarship about a major poet. The essay offers a complete annotated bibliography organized by decade, listing every book and article with a one-sentence summary. What does the essay lack to become field-defining?
questions.answer: An argument about which assumptions in the scholarship should be abandoned and what should replace them.
choices: An argument about which assumptions in the scholarship should be abandoned and what should replace them.
Coverage of scholarship published in languages other than the essayist's own.
A concluding section listing the archives and manuscripts that remain unexamined.
An alphabetical index of the works discussed so readers can find them quickly.
