questions.skill: Rethinking print culture as a social achievement rather than a technical one
questions.prompt: Elizabeth Eisenstein argued that printing in fifteenth-century Europe produced standardized, fixed texts and so transformed knowledge. Adrian Johns's study of the early modern English book trade replies that the first printers' output was full of unauthorized editions, garbled texts, and disputes over credit. What is the core of Johns's objection?
questions.answer: Print's fixity and credibility were not automatic properties of the technology; they had to be produced by institutions, conventions, and law.
choices: Print's fixity and credibility were not automatic properties of the technology; they had to be produced by institutions, conventions, and law.
Eisenstein's account is wrong because printing spread far more slowly in England than on the continent.
The thesis fails because print never displaced manuscript, so printed and handwritten texts must be edited apart from one another.
The early book trade was too small in scale to have affected how knowledge was produced in the period.

questions.skill: Stating what computational counting can and cannot demonstrate
questions.prompt: A research team uses a full-text database of British novels to count occurrences of the word "sentimental" between 1780 and 1860. The counts rise steeply after 1830, and the team concludes that Victorian culture became more sentimental. Which objection most directly limits the conclusion drawn from the counts?
questions.answer: The counts record how often a word occurs in the sampled texts; they do not establish what the word meant in those texts or how anyone responded to it.
choices: The counts record how often a word occurs in the sampled texts; they do not establish what the word meant in those texts or how anyone responded to it.
A program cannot read literature, so results produced by counting words must be set aside in advance.
The conclusion would hold only if the same pattern appeared in every individual novel in the database, since a pattern spread across many texts proves nothing about any of them.
The counts cannot support any claim about the period, because they were made from a database rather than from the printed books themselves.

questions.skill: Translating research evidence into standards and seeing its limits
questions.prompt: A national ministry asks a panel of reading researchers to write standards for primary reading instruction. The panel's evidence review includes controlled experimental studies of beginning reading but excludes classroom-observation studies and studies of reading comprehension beyond the sentence level. What is the strongest statement of the problem this creates for the standards?
questions.answer: The standards will be well supported on the questions the included studies answer and thin on the ones they leave out, so schools will have to fill the gaps on their own.
choices: The standards will be well supported on the questions the included studies answer and thin on the ones they leave out, so schools will have to fill the gaps on their own.
Standards drawn from experimental studies cannot be applied in classrooms, because teaching never resembles the conditions of an experiment.
Excluding any study from a review makes the resulting standards invalid, so the standards should be withdrawn.
Classroom-observation studies are always more reliable than experiments and should therefore replace them in the review.

questions.skill: Applying global history-of-the-book frameworks
questions.prompt: A historian of the book studies how readers in colonial-era Manila used printed books imported from Spain alongside handwritten religious texts produced locally in several Philippine languages. Which conclusion best fits the evidence that both forms circulated together?
questions.answer: The arrival of print did not simply replace manuscript practice but produced a mixed economy of reading.
choices: The arrival of print did not simply replace manuscript practice but produced a mixed economy of reading.
Printed books were treated as more authoritative than handwritten texts in every context.
Manuscript production increased only where the Spanish authorities banned printing.
Local languages were used only for handwriting, never for printed books.

questions.skill: Assessing what digital corpus studies can claim about literary influence
questions.prompt: A computational study builds a database of twentieth-century novels in translation and reports that novels from Country A are far more often translated than novels from Country B. The study concludes that Country A's literature is more influential worldwide. What is the strongest objection?
questions.answer: Translation depends on publishing markets, funding, and political ties, not only on literary influence.

questions.skill: Critiquing cross-country comparisons in international reading assessments
questions.prompt: A newspaper reports that Country X's average score on the PISA reading assessment is lower than Country Y's, and concludes that Country X's reading teachers are less effective. Which is the strongest reason the conclusion does not follow from the report?
questions.answer: A country mean on an assessment of 15-year-olds reflects home language, migration, who is still enrolled in school at 15, and the curriculum, not the quality of teaching alone.
choices: A country mean on an assessment of 15-year-olds reflects home language, migration, who is still enrolled in school at 15, and the curriculum, not the quality of teaching alone.
PISA reports only the share of students at each proficiency level and never reports country mean scores.
Reading achievement is largely inherited, so differences between countries cannot reflect instruction at all.
PISA scores are reported on a scale with no fixed reference points, so countries cannot be placed in the same order.

questions.skill: Critiquing claims drawn from large international reading assessments
questions.prompt: A ministry statement reads: "Between 2016 and 2021 our fourth-year students' mean score on the large international reading assessment rose by 18 points, while our neighbor's fell by 5. This proves our new national reading standards work better than theirs." Which evaluation of this claim is best?
questions.answer: The claim is not supported: the assessments compare successive cohorts of students on a common scaled construct, and no element of the design isolates the effect of any country's standards or instruction.

The claim is supported: these assessments exist precisely to rank national systems and to show which country's policies are the most effective.
The claim is supported: because the score difference is statistically significant, the new standards rather than chance produced the change.
The claim is not supported, but only because the two countries tested different grade levels and so their results cannot be compared at all.

questions.skill: Judging the scope of an evidence claim in the reading wars
questions.prompt: A state legislator is told: "The National Reading Panel's meta-analysis of experimental studies found that systematic phonics instruction produced larger gains in word reading, spelling, and in some conditions text comprehension than non-systematic or no phonics, with the clearest advantages in kindergarten and first grade and for children at risk of reading difficulty." A witness replies: "Then the research shows that phonics is all a reading program needs." Which reason best shows that the witness's conclusion does not follow?
questions.answer: The comparison set systematic phonics against non-systematic or no phonics, and the Panel concluded that phonics should be one part of a complete reading program.
choices: The comparison set systematic phonics against non-systematic or no phonics, and the Panel concluded that phonics should be one part of a complete reading program.
Meta-analysis cannot settle questions about teaching, because it averages studies that differ from one another.
The Panel found no measurable advantage for systematic phonics in any grade or group of children.
Phonics instruction has been shown to help only children learning to read in languages other than English.

questions.skill: Interpreting international assessment results cautiously
questions.prompt: An international reading assessment reports that students in Country A score higher on literary response items than on informational text items, while Country B shows the reverse. A researcher concludes that Country A's teachers are better at teaching literary response. What is the strongest objection?
questions.answer: Differences between the two item types may reflect the passages and tasks used, not what teachers taught.
choices: Differences between the two item types may reflect the passages and tasks used, not what teachers taught.
Country B has more students learning to read in a second language than Country A does.
The assessment tested more informational items than literary response items.
National samples cannot show what individual teachers did in their classrooms.

questions.skill: International Literacy Assessments and Comparative Reading Achievement — Reading
questions.prompt: A large international assessment reports country results for the reading achievement of fifteen-year-olds. Country A's mean score is 523 and Country B's is 491. A ministry in Country A cites the 32-point gap as proof that its schools teach reading better than Country B's. Which fact most directly undercuts that claim?
questions.answer: Country A left about a quarter of its fifteen-year-olds outside the tested population, including most students in vocational and special-education tracks, while Country B left out fewer than three percent.

Country B's mean rose 11 points since the previous cycle while Country A's stayed level, so the comparison sets an improving system against a stagnant one and proves nothing.
